absaetze.t: Kursverluste erwartet DAX fällt vor US-Midterms wohl zurück

Vor den US-Zwischenwahlen sind die Anleger nervös. Der DAX dürfte zum Handelsstart zurückfallen. Auch die Quartalsbilanz von Apple ist Gesprächsthema am Markt. Der Ausblick enttäuschte die Erwartungen.

Der Broker IG Markets taxiert den deutschen Leitindex vor der Eröffnung des Xetra-Handels 0,8 Prozent tiefer auf 25.781 Punkte. Zu Wochenbeginn war der DAX 0,6 Prozent höher bei 25.981 Punkten aus dem Handel gegangen. Die Marke von 26.000 Punkten erweist sich aktuell als hohe Hürde.

Laut dem Experten Salah-Eddine Bouhmidi vom Broker IG fehlte den Anlegern noch die nachhaltige Überzeugung, um sie zu überwinden. "Politische Klarheit könnte dafür den Anstoß geben - geopolitische Risiken bleiben allerdings ein Unsicherheitsfaktor", gibt er mit Blick auf die Zwischenwahlen in den USA zu bedenken.
US-Zwischenwahlen bestimmen den Handelstag

In den Zwischenwahlen entscheidet sich, ob die Demokraten der Republikanischen Partei von Präsident Donald Trump die Kontrolle über den Kongress entreißen können. Umfragen deuten darauf hin, dass die Demokraten das Repräsentantenhaus gewinnen, während der Ausgang im Senat unklarer ist.

Viele Investoren fürchten, dass die USA nach den Wahlen einen erneuten Angriff auf Iran planen, mit schlimmen Folgen für den Rohstoffmarkt und die Weltkonjunktur. Allerdings antwortete Trump jüngst auf die Frage von Reportern, ob er einen Angriff auf Iran nach den Zwischenwahlen in Betracht ziehe, mit "Nein". Er glaube zudem, dass Iran eine Einigung erzielen wolle und dass eine solche Vereinbarung auch "zustande kommen könnte".

"Die Gefahr eines erneuten US-Militärschlags ist zwar längst nicht vom Tisch", sagte Thomas Altmann, Portfoliomanager beim Vermögensverwalter QC Partners. Aber die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass dieser unmittelbar nach den Midterms erfolge, sei deutlich gesunken.
Apples Ausblick enttäuscht

Auch die Bilanzsaison bleibt ein wesentlicher Faktor für Kursbewegungen. Geht die KI-Wette auf? Das ist eine der Fragen, die die Anleger derzeit am meisten umtreiben. Deshalb achten sie besonders auf die Ergebnisse der US-Tech-Konzerne. Am Montag nach US-Börsenschluss ließ sich Apple in die Bücher schauen.

Die Anleger bekamen Licht und Schatten zu sehen. Der iPhone-Umsatz und die gesamten Konzernerlöse erreichten zwar Rekordwerte für ein September-Quartal. Unter dem Strich blieben mehr als 30 Milliarden Dollar hängen. Aber an der Börse werden nun mal vor allem die Erwartungen für die Zukunft gehandelt: Die Anleger reagierten enttäuscht auf die Prognose für das laufende Quartal.
KI-Datenfirma Palantir wächst weiter

Auch die Datenanalyse-Firma Palantir stellte Quartalszahlen vor. Der Umsatz stieg im dritten Quartal im Jahresvergleich um 96 Prozent auf 2,3 Milliarden Dollar. Unter dem Strich wuchs der Gewinn um 49 Prozent auf 1,13 Milliarden Dollar.

Palantir ist auf die Auswertung großer Datenmengen spezialisiert und liefert unter anderem Software, mit der Geheimdienst- und Militär-Informationen analysiert werden. Das Geschäft mit amerikanischen Regierungsbehörden wuchs um 96 Prozent auf 953 Millionen Dollar. Software von Palantir wird unter anderem vom Heimatschutzministerium und vom Pentagon eingesetzt, Medienberichten zufolge auch im Iran-Krieg.

items.titel: A Nuclear Strike On Iran? It Sounds Absurd Because It Is. Let’s Talk About It
items.anriss: On Sunday evening, commentator Tucker Carlson made a chilling claim : U.S. President Donald Trump may soon use nuclear weapons against Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain facility . Carlson’s comments were posted on X just two days ahead of the Nov. 3 …

absaetze.t: On Sunday evening, commentator Tucker Carlson made a chilling claim: U.S. President Donald Trump may soon use nuclear weapons against Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain facility. Carlson’s comments were posted on X just two days ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, which Trump has frequently used as a timeframe for when he would conduct a new wave of airstrikes on Iran if he so decides. However, earlier on Monday, Trump downplayed that deadline, answering “no” when asked by reporters whether he was considering attacking after the election is over.

Regardless, Carlson’s claim runs counter to the president’s previous stance on the nuclear weapons issue. Trump has publicly eschewed their use, and while he has discussed attacking Pickaxe Mountain, he’s made it clear it would be by a conventional weapon if he made the call.
Monday afternoon, the White House dismissed Carlson’s asssertion.

“President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe,” a White House official told us. “Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief’s thinking.”

We don’t know the source of Carlson’s information or if it is in any way accurate. Carlson has experienced a major rift with Trump and has said plenty of shocking things in recent years, especially in regard to Trump’s second term and the war with Iran. Still, he is a very connected figure in right-wing media. Regardless, as TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway noted on X, even conjecture that has gone viral about the potential use of a nuclear weapon for the first time since the U.S. bombed Nagasaki on Aug. 9, 1945, merits discussion. It would have such profound and irrevocable repercussions that it should not be ignored. We addressed the same concerns in regard to Russia and Ukraine in 2022.

“If a nuclear weapon were used on [Pickaxe Mountain] in Iran by the US or Israel or an empty field in Ukraine by Russia etc, it doesn’t matter, it would open up Pandora’s box and would make the U.S. and the world dramatically less safe,” Rogoway stated. “This isn’t even a question of how big of a disaster the use, in any manner, of a nuclear weapon would be. It would represent the largest foreign policy error ever by the United States if we were involved. We can only hope this claim isn’t accurate in any way.”
“…And I have no idea if this claim has merit, but this is important nonetheless,” he added in his X thread. “It is massively viral on my X feed. It has to be addressed.”

Pickaxe Mountain, a very hardened Iranian facility also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is located in central Iran. As we have noted previously, it is deeply buried and would be a very difficult target to effectively destroy. In the past, Iran has openly discussed plans to produce centrifuges to support its nuclear enrichment efforts at the newer facility located there. It is also estimated to be large enough to house an actual enrichment plant, as well as other nuclear infrastructure, but exactly what is inside remains unconfirmed. Our previous reporting provides deeper insights into Pickaxe Mountain and Iran’s possible intentions for it.
What Carlson said

“Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran,” Carlson stated on X. “The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place.”

“The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one,” the commentator added. “‘Bibi calls Trump about it every day,’ says an informed observer. Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.”
What Trump has said about using nuclear weapons

“We don’t need it. Why do I need it?” Trump responded in April when asked if he would use nuclear weapons against Iran. “Why would a stupid question like that be asked? Why would I use a nuclear weapon where we’ve totally in a very conventional way decimated them without it.”
“A nuclear weapon should never be allowed to be used by anybody,” he added.
The American leader reiterated that stance in August.

“They’re totally defeated militarily, so I defeat them, and now I should use a nuclear weapon on top of them? What a stupid question,” Trump responded on Aug. 31 when again asked by a reporter if he would use nuclear weapons against Iran.
Still, Trump sparked concerns about whether he would use nuclear weapons when he threatened to obliterate Iran in April in a social media post.
“A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” Trump stated on his Truth Social site. “I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”
Several experts we spoke with downplayed the chances that Trump would order a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain, but they did not completely rule it out.

“Is it likely? No,” Daryl G. Kimball, Executive Director of the Arms Control Association (ACA) and publisher and contributor for the organization’s monthly journal, Arms Control Today, said when we asked if he thought Trump would order a nuclear strike. “Is it possible that an unstable desperate president who has sole authority to authorize nuclear weapons use, would do so, yes. Given the situation, it is crucial that responsible U.S. voices and international leaders speak out against a massive U.S. strike on Iran of any kind.”

“That is highly unlikely,” Hans Kristensen — director, Nuclear Information Project, Federation of American Scientists, explained to us. He also writes the bi-monthly Nuclear Notebook and the world nuclear forces overview in the SIPRI Yearbook. “There is nothing at all in Iran that justifies breaking the 81-year absence of nuclear weapons use. It would be a violation of the international Laws of War, have devastating consequences for U.S. foreign policy and the efforts to prevent proliferation and the use of nuclear weapons. It would be the kind of act where one would hope the people in the nuclear chain of command would refuse to carry out the president’s order.”

“I honestly don’t know that anyone knows that Trump will or won’t do, including Trump,” Stephen I. Schwartz, nonresident senior fellow at the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, told us. “… for many years, often without prompting, he has spoken with a mix of wariness and awe about the tremendous power of nuclear weapons. But he has also publicly and repeatedly threatened to utterly annihilate North Korea, Afghanistan, and Iran. So, really, who knows?”
What weapon could the U.S. use if Trump ordered a nuclear strike?
As we have reported in the past, the B61-11 is the only air-delivered nuclear weapon in the U.S. stockpile today that is specifically designed to address this target set.

“The B61-11 is based on the earlier B61-7, but is substantially different in form and function. It has a heavily reinforced outer shell, possibly with a depleted uranium penetrating nose section, and a rocket booster at the rear to help it penetrate down into underground facilities. Sources differ on the maximum yield of the B61-11, but it is said to either be between 340 and 360 kilotons (identical to that of the B61-7) or to be closer to 400 kilotons. There are also reportedly fewer than 100 of these bombs in the stockpile.”
The first B61-11 versions entered service in the 1960s. We have written extensively about the entire family of these weapons.

Given the yield of the B61-11, “one could probably do the job” of rendering Pickaxe Mountain unusable, Kristensen told us. “The collateral damage from 400 kilotons would be considerable; even if some very deep structures potentially survived, the damage to the overall infrastructure — plus the residual radiation in the soil — would probably make the site unusable. Other potential options include more conventional penetrator attacks to take out access points and accessible infrastructure, or potentially cyber attacks to sabotage or disable equipment and functions.”

“I think there are many non-nuclear options the United States and/or Israel could utilize to prevent Iran from restarting its nuclear weapons program (if, indeed, Iran has made a decision to do that),” argued Schwartz. “That would include using guided conventional bombs to target any entrances to the facility, impeding efforts of personnel to gain access and also complicating/preventing the movement of any materials out of the mountain.”

“Using an ICBM [intercontinental ballistic missile] would not be a good option,” he added. “For one thing, any ICBM would have to fly over Russia to reach Iran, which would be risky in more ways than one, even if Putin somehow agreed to allow that to happen. For another, ICBM warheads are not designed to penetrate the earth, at least not to any significant depth, so the force of the explosion would largely be ‘wasted’ on the surface, with everything that implies about lethal radioactive fallout. (Using an SLBM [submarine-launched ballistic missile] from a Trident submarine stationed closer to Iran would avoid the overflight risks but would also still be perceived as a threat by Russia and perhaps China after launch, even if we notify them in advance. But W76 and W76-1 warheads are not earth-penetrators, and I doubt we would want to use a 455-kiloton W88, our largest ballistic missile warhead, also not a deep earth-penetrator.)”
Israel has a nuclear weapons program that it does not publicly acknowledge and can deliver warheads via its Jericho ballistic missiles, some tactical jets and maybe even submarines.

It’s possible a special operations forces teams could attempt to raid the facility, access its interior and place a nuclear device inside it, although such a mission would be immensely challenging and extremely risky. We have also talked about the possibility of irradiating the facilities from the inside without using a nuclear warhead, but instead planting and detonating a kind of dirty bomb.
What are the alternatives to nuclear weapons?
As we noted earlier in this story, Trump has brought up the issue of conventional weapons to attack Pickaxe Mountain. In July, he said it was ripe for a “nice big fat shot right in the front door.”
At the time, we discussed how difficult it would be to effectively destroy or render inoperable a hardened, deeply buried facility like Pickaxe.

For years, experts have talked about the likelihood that the main caverns under the mountain are beyond the reach of even the largest known conventional bunker buster bomb in U.S. inventory, the 30,000-pound-class GBU-57/B Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP). The MOP was developed, at least in part, specifically to hold underground facilities in Iran at risk. Construction at Pickaxe Mountain, especially in the past five years, is a clear response to U.S. threats.

items.titel: Counter-Drone Laser Weapon Now Guarding Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Alongside SAMs
items.anriss: At least one AeroVironment LOCUST laser counter-drone system is part of the array of anti-air defenses that have popped up around President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, in recent weeks. Versions of LOCUST have …

absaetze.t: At least one AeroVironment LOCUST laser counter-drone system is part of the array of anti-air defenses that have popped up around President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, in recent weeks. Versions of LOCUST have been seeing steadily increasing use within the U.S. military in recent years, including deployments now along the border with Mexico. Though there has been much progress in the development of practical laser directed-energy weapons in recent years, the technology has continued to face hurdles to more widespread adoption.

The LOCUST system at Mar-a-Lago, which is mounted on a 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV), is seen in two pictures that Getty’s Andrew Harnik took on October 31. When exactly the laser-directed energy weapon was deployed is unclear. Laser Wars was the first to spot the system in one of Harnik’s pictures and confirm its deployment.

Harnik’s main focus was a pair of Humvee-based AN/TWQ-1 Avenger short-range air defense systems on a floating platform in Lake Worth Lagoon near the edge of the estate, which were first deployed there just over two weeks ago. Additional Avengers have also been positioned around Donald J. Trump International Airport, which is situated some three miles to the west. The U.S. military has also set up elements of Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System Fly-Away Kits, including Ku-band radar, electronic support measures (ESM), jammers, and 360-degree infrared search and track systems nearby. TWZ covered the presence of the Avengers and the Fly-Away Kits in a report last Friday.

This heightened security comes amid signs that a new round of major hostilities with Iran could be on the horizon, as well as the run-up to tomorrow’s mid-term elections. The regime in Tehran has threatened Trump’s life on several occasions over the years. The President has already been the subject of several domestic assassination attempts and threats.

“At the request of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and under NORAD [the U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command] and USNORTHCOM [U.S. Northern Command] authorities, NORAD and USNORTHCOM recently deployed ground-based air defense [GBAD] assets and Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in and around Mar-a-Lago, Florida,” the commands told us in a statement last week. “These assets add a complementary layer of technology to enhance protection. Due to operational security, we are unable to provide additional details. For further detail, we refer you to the USSS.”

“The U.S. Secret Service is operating in a heightened threat environment, and we continuously adapt our protective operations to incorporate cutting-edge tools, technology, and methods to safeguard our protectees,” the Secret Service also told us in a prior statement. “At the request of the U.S. Secret Service, NORAD and U.S. Northern Command are providing Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in support of our protective operations.”

The U.S. Army began receiving the JLTV-based versions of LOCUST, along with examples mounted on the smaller 4×4 Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV) last year through a program called the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL). This followed the delivery of palletized LOCUST systems under a rapid prototyping effort called the Palletized-High Energy Laser (P-HEL) in the early 2020s. The Army is now acquiring LOCUST X3 systems under its Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program. LOCUST has become something of a star more broadly within the directed energy space across the U.S. military. The U.S. Marine Corps and the U.S. Navy have also been exploring the use of versions of LOCUST in ground-based and shipboard contexts.

To date, all versions of LOCUST consist of a turret with the laser beam projector, as well as built-in electro-optical and infrared video cameras for target acquisition and tracking. The complete system also includes power generation and cooling components. LOCUST variants can also be cued using offboard sensors, including small-form-factor high-frequency radars and passive radio frequency signal detection systems on host vehicles or located off-platform nearby, like what the Fly-Away Kit provides.

The stated power rating for LOCUST varies from version to version, with the latest X3 being a 30-kilowatt type. Though the system is categorized as a high-energy laser, this is at the lower end of the power spectrum for weapons of this type, and it is explicitly geared toward the countering small drones mission set. Layering LOCUST in with other hard- and soft-kill counter-drone and air defense systems in a potentially high-threat area, as we are seeing now at Mar-a-Lago, makes good sense.

As mentioned, Mar-a-Lago is not the first time a LOCUST has been deployed in a real-world context. In 2022, the Army confirmed the operational deployment of two P-HEL systems to unspecified foreign locales. Earlier this year, JLTV- and ISV-based AMP-HELs have appeared along the border with Mexico. One of the systems was part of the chain of events that led to the shutdown of airspace around El Paso, Texas, in February. That incident, in turn, prompted the Pentagon to craft a new agreement with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regarding the use of laser directed energy weapons within the United States.
As TWZ has written in the past:

“In general, laser directed energy weapons offer the promise of functionally unlimited magazine depth, as long as there is sufficient power and cooling capacity. They also present a drastically lower cost-per-intercept proposition compared to traditional anti-air interceptors. This is all advantageous for engaging drones, particularly smaller and cheaper designs that can still present very significant threats. The dangers posed by uncrewed aerial systems are only set to grow as networked swarming and automated targeting capabilities, enabled by advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning, become more accessible. Defenders already face real risks of just being overwhelmed by attacks involving volumes of drones.”

“At the same time, a laser like LOCUST can only engage a single target at once. Lower-powered lasers need to dwell on their targets for a longer period of time in order to cause significant damage by burning a hole in them, as well. This limits the number of targets a single system can engage in a given window of time.”

“In addition, the power of any laser beam drops as it propagates through the atmosphere further and further away from its source. Weather and other environmental factors like smoke and dust can also distort the beam and reduce its power. All of this only adds to the aforementioned dwell time. Adaptive optics, and just more power overall, can help produce useful effects at greater distances, but laser weapons continue to have short ranges, typically measured in handfuls of miles, as a general rule.”

“The Army, as well as other branches of the U.S. military, have repeatedly acknowledged challenges in fielding laser directed energy weapon systems. Sensitivity to vibration, humidity, dust, and sand, as well as fragile optics and cooling demands, have all created further complications for operating and sustaining these systems in real-world environments. “

Army officials just recently touted the benefits of laser directed energy weapons like LOCUST, while also acknowledging again that there is still work to be done at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention last month.

“Lasers are real. We can do it. We can go out. We can shoot things,” Kirk Williams, Chief Engineer at the Army’s Directed Energy Project Office, another one of the panelists, said. “But what we got to do now is make these systems reliable enough so that the soldiers have the faith in them when they need them, and that’s really the main point that we’re trying to go after right now.”

“We’re getting to the point where the systems are reliable enough, but we still have to make them maintainable and repairable because this is an Army system,” he continued. “It’s going to be on a battlefield. Things are going to break. We can break things in very creative ways, right? So if it’s not reliable, or if it’s not maintainable, if it’s not repairable, that’s a problem.”
At least one LOCUST system is now participating in a very high-profile mission to help protect President Trump.
Contact the author: joe@twz.com

items.titel: Boy Friends

absaetze.t: Die Figuren Gian, Milo und Peter (v.l.n.r.) in full action ©junges theater basel

Drei Jungen stehen vor einer Klasse. «Mir sind do, wäg dem Vorfall vo vorletschte Wuche.» - «Mir händ nüt demit z’ tue.» - «Aber …» Sie sind mehr oder weniger freiwillig da. Aber immerhin sind sie da. Und sie versuchen, mit der Klasse – oder zunächst vielleicht eher mit sich selbst – ins Gespräch zu kommen. von Janina Labhardt
Im Neuen Theater Basel läuft "Boy Friends, handle with care"
Was bedeutet Respekt? Wer sind unsere Vorbilder? Wo endet Freundschaft, wo beginnt Verantwortung? Und was hat das alles mit Männlichkeit zu tun?

Das junge theater basel bringt mit der Produktion "Boy Friends - handle with care" Töne zum Schwingen, die mit den drei Schauspielern Yuri Fasola, Loris Mongillo und Luzius Andreetti eine perfekte Ressonanz finden. Die tiefsinnigen Überlegungen und die Auseinandersetzung mit dem Thema Männlichkeit sind echt, überzeugend und glaubwürdig.

Lehrpersonen können das Theaterstück buchen, sodass also das junge theater basel ins Klassenzimmer kommt. Im Anschluss an die Vorstellungen bietet das jung theater basel einen Workshop mit dem Männerbüro Basel.
Das Stück "Boy Friends" läuft noch bis zum 27. November im jungen theater basel, an der Kasernenstrasse 23 in Basel.

items.titel: À Paris, Vannes ou Nantes, 5 expos gratuites à voir au mois de novembre
items.anriss: Dans une nouvelle galerie à Nantes, un tiers-lieu culturel à Vannes, une fondation à Paris… Comme chaque mois, Beaux Arts vous propose sa sélection d’expositions gratuites à voir en France, pour un mois de novembre placé sous le signe de …

absaetze.t: Comme de coutume, le mois de novembre sera photographique ou ne sera pas. Outre la foire Paris Photo au Grand Palais, de très nombreuses expositions gratuites se visitent sur tout le territoire. Nous vous avons par exemple déjà parlé de la biennale de la Petite Photographie, micro-expo de onze photographes travaillant le (très) petit format dans une galerie du 6e arrondissement de Paris.

On notera aussi le très riche agenda de Photo Days, qui fédère des expositions dans des dizaines de galeries et d’institutions où l’entrée est libre, comme chez Jean-François Cazeau, à la galerie du jour, chez Polka ou chez Thaddaeus Ropac, ou encore au Centre culturel canadien, au Quai de la photo ou au Lavoir numérique. Et sinon ? Suivez le guide !
À Vannes, un tout nouveau tiers-lieu culturel de 600 m2

Bonne nouvelle pour les Bretons ! Malgré la fermeture imminente pour déménagement du musée de La Cohue à Vannes, les amateurs d’art actuel peuvent désormais fréquenter La Traverse, tiers-lieu culturel qui métamorphose les anciens bureaux de la direction départementale des Territoires et de la Mer (DDTM) en un vaste parcours artistique de 600 m2, installé sur la rive gauche du port de Vannes. Cet automne, on y découvre ainsi les œuvres de dix-neuf artistes contemporains et urbains – Jean Faucheur, Amandine Urruty, Isaac Cordal ou Broken Fingaz –, chacun investissant une pièce du bâtiment. La Traverse est également un lieu de vie à part entière, avec un bar, une terrasse sur le port, des ateliers d’artistes et même une salle de théâtre et de cinéma. Tous à Vannes !
Dialogie. De l’éclaircie à l’horizon

À la fondation EDF, quand la lumière se met à danser

Bonne nouvelle : l’excitante exploration transdisciplinaire « Dans(e) la lumière » revient pour une troisième édition à la fondation EDF, dans le 7e arrondissement de Paris. Comme à chaque fois, artistes et chorégraphes sont réunis dans une programmation qui allie exposition (gratuite donc), événements et spectacles de danse (payants quant à eux), pour analyser la façon dont des œuvres d’aujourd’hui revisitent les possibles de la lumière. En continu, on pourra découvrir l’installation vidéo inédite de l’artiste Tiler Gab et de la danseuse Nùria Guiu Sagarra, intitulée Keep Dancing, dans laquelle le visiteur, guidé par la lumière, peut danser, rêver ou même faire du yoga sur une création musicale de Thomas Vaquié. L’agenda compte aussi des créationsde Blanca Li, Noé Chapsal, Helena Olmedo ou Maud Le Pladec, ainsi que des performances de jeunes chorégraphes issus du dispositif « IADU » (Initiatives d’artistes en danses urbaines).

À Nantes, une nouvelle galerie pour l’art contemporain

C’est une belle histoire, que nous avons déjà racontée dans nos pages : en 2021, à Nantes, une mère et son fils de 23 ans décident d’ouvrir une galerie exclusivement dédiée à la redécouverte d’artistes négligés par la grande histoire de l’art, la galerie des Oubliés. Cette année, Léopold Cottineau poursuit sa conquête du marché de l’art en inaugurant – toujours à Nantes – la galerie Angelo, dédiée à la scène contemporaine. Pour sa première exposition, le jeune homme ne dévie pas tout à fait de sa trajectoire familiale puisqu’il décide d’exposer une trentaine de peintures de sa propre mère (et associée, donc), Izabeau Jousse (née en 1967). Celle-ci n’avait rien présenté au public depuis une dizaine d’années, et dévoile des compositions géométriques à l’intense palette chromatique, où, explique-t-elle, « apparaissent des femmes paisibles qui déploient leurs jambes vers l’extérieur et réfugient leur visage dans leurs mains, ferment les yeux pour se cacher un peu ».

À Clichy et Senlis, 100 photographies réunies par la fondation Francès

Ils n’ont pas froid aux yeux. « L’art est juste lorsqu’il nous invite à réfléchir, à frémir, à infléchir nos points de vue. Lorsqu’il nous pousse aussi parfois à déglutir ou à vomir », déclarent le couple de collectionneurs Estelle et Hervé Francès sur le site de leur fondation. Pour le bicentenaire de la photographie, la grande exposition qu’ils organisent dans leurs deux espaces, à Senlis et à Clichy, ne fait pas exception à cette ambition, et témoigne encore une fois de la force des œuvres qu’ils achètent depuis exactement 20 ans. Sous le commissariat d’Estelle Francès, celle-ci se divise en deux chapitres, axés sur la photographie et le cinéma à Senlis et sur le corps à Clichy, et réunit des images qui, détaille la collectionneuse, « disent autant de nous que des artistes qui les ont faites. Le bicentenaire était le moment de partager ce qui, jusqu’ici, restait entre nous. »
Faire corps. Vingt ans de photographie dans la collection Francès à Senlis

À Paris, la Maison Gacha met à l’honneur le patrimoine camerounais du ndop

C’est un lieu singulier, qui a ouvert ses portes il y a bientôt deux ans rue des Épinettes, dans le 17e arrondissement. Sur l’initiative de Ly Dumas, la Maison Gacha a été créée pour valoriser « les savoir-faire et les métiers de la main d’Afrique et d’ailleurs ». Sa nouvelle exposition entre dans les secrets du ndop, un textile teint en blanc et bleu paré de motifs, dont les savoir-faire circulent entre le Cameroun et le Nigeria. Autrefois attribut du pouvoir royal, y apprend-on, celui-ci se trouve aujourd’hui largement diffusé grâce à une production industrielle, son histoire reflétant les évolutions du monde. Le parcours réunit de fascinantes œuvres bamoun, bamiléké et wukari, dont des costumes, des accessoires et des masques. À voir !

absaetze.t: En marge de Paris Photo, du 12 au 15 novembre 2026, St'Art célèbre sa trentième édition à Strasbourg avec la première Strasbourg Art Week, tandis qu'Approche fête ses dix ans et que Signatures Art Fair fait ses débuts à Paris.

Chaque mois de novembre, Paris vit au rythme de la photographie, avec Paris Photo, qui réunit les grandes galeries internationales sous la nef du Grand Palais. La rédaction a retenu trois autres rendez-vous qui élargissent le regard : à Strasbourg, St’Art mêle art contemporain, art verrier et estampe ; à Paris, Approche expérimente avec l’image et Signatures Art Fair consacre l’œuvre éditée.
1. Approche : la photographie comme matière vivante

Emilia Genuardi, fondatrice d’Approche, a toujours envisagé la photographie sous l’angle de l’expérimentation. Pour les 10 ans du salon, elle garde cette « conception de l’image comme une matière vivante qui peut être pliée, couturée, dorée, fossilisée, érodée… », davantage qu’implantée dans un marché, même si ce dernier a bien fonctionné jusqu’à présent. Ce sont les artistes qui attirent son œil, à l’exemple de Jérémie Lenoir (pour la galerie Capazza), Manon Lanjouère (Galerie du jour agnès b.) ou Sido Lansari (Proche). En lien avec le bicentenaire de la photographie, la photo plus historique est célébrée, avec les photomontages des années 1920 du Berlinois Heinz Hajek-Halke (chez Chaussée 36 Photography), ou une rétrospective des recherches menées par Jean-Pierre Sudre, dès 1949 (Quand les fleurs nous sauvent).
Heinz Hajek-Halke, Komposition 4/56 (Composition 4/6), 1956 épreuve gélatino-argentique, Lichtgrafik 30.7 x 21.7 cm. Pièce unique © Heinz Hajek-Halke, Courtesy Chaussée 36
2. St’Art au cœur de la Strasbourg Art Week

Pour sa trentième édition, et malgré un contexte qui n’a pas toujours été facile, St’Art reçoit une soixantaine de galeries françaises et européennes, dont 17 nouvelles venues. Carole Schaller, responsable du développement de la foire, attribue ce succès à l’alliance entre les secteurs publics et privés. « Notre ancrage sur le territoire alsacien et la nouvelle municipalité de Catherine Trautmann nous apportent un grand soutien, qui a permis de lancer la Strasbourg Art Week. Cette dernière fédère les institutions, comme le FRAC Alsace, le musée d’Art moderne et contemporain, le musée Würth, ainsi que le mouvement de coopération l’Industrie Magnifique et des entreprises privées. Puis, au sein de la foire, nous n’oublions pas notre mission éducative, notamment par des visites pédagogiques. » Aux fidèles galeries Kraemer de Strasbourg, Murmure de Colmar, JustBEE de Masevaux, Arnoux de Paris ou encore Pigment de Barcelone, se joignent deux exposants de Roumanie, Anaid Art et Gloriae. Pour la première fois, St’Art dépasse les murs du Parc des expositions avec la Strasbourg Art Week, du 10 au 15 novembre : un parcours dans la ville, sans vocation commerciale.
Madar Réka, Shoes, 2012, huile sur toile, 70 x 80 cm, Estopia
3. Signatures Art Fair : vive les éditions limitées !

Signatures Art Fair fait ses débuts au Carreau du Temple. Ce salon dédié à l’art moderne et contemporain en édition limitée, de 1945 à nos jours, entend redonner une place de choix à l’œuvre originale éditée : estampes, photographies, sculptures, livres d’artistes, mais aussi objets et mobilier. Fondatrice du projet, Carine Tissot, qui est aussi directrice du salon Drawing Now, voulait « donner à ces œuvres un rendez-vous à part entière ». Elle a réuni une quarantaine de galeries et d’éditeurs français ou étrangers, dont Pierre-Alain Challier, Perrotin, Almine Rech et Semiose, avec des prix de 50 € à plus de 100 000 €. Ambassadeur du salon, l’architecte Karl Fournier (Studio KO) signe une sélection, « L’Œil de KO », avec notamment Lynn Chadwick, Nina Childress et Xie Lei.

items.titel: Batek Architekten designs Berlin orthodontic clinic that looks more like a boutique or gallery
items.anriss: Avoiding the sterile appearance of most medical interiors, Berlin-based Batek Architekten used soothing shades of pastel yellow and matt silver to bring a sense of softness to orthodontic clinic Hey.

absaetze.t: Avoiding the sterile appearance of most medical interiors, Berlin-based Batek Architekten used soothing shades of pastel yellow and matt silver to bring a sense of softness to orthodontic clinic Hey.
Described by its designers as “quietly playful”, Hey combines its two-tone palette with bold geometric elements.
These include a folded steel reception counter, a sculptural bench, and a criss-cross coat rail.
Treatment rooms feature translucent walls of glass-fibre-reinforced plastic, while lighting tubes trace graphic lines across the ceiling.
The result is a space that could be mistaken for a high-end fashion boutique or an art gallery.
“We decided early on to work almost monochromatically,” said studio founder Patrick Batek.
“A soft pastel yellow runs from the floor up across the walls, enveloping visitors and creating a warm, comforting atmosphere.”

Batek Architekten‘s scheme, overseen by Batek and architect Julia Jensen, evolved from a brief set by the client, doctor Julie Charlotte Angrick, who wanted a clinic where young patients would feel comfortable.
It was this that led Angrick to name it Hey, intended as an informal welcome.
“Most visitors are children and teenagers, and many of them come regularly over several years,” explained Batek.
“We wanted to create a place that takes away the fear of the clinical environment without being childish,” he told Dezeen.
“Instead of colourful decoration, we chose radical reduction.”
The same thinking shaped the visual identity developed by graphic design studio Bailey und Bailey, which includes a logo incorporating a smiley face emoticon.
The visual aesthetic didn’t come at the expense of functionality or hygiene.

Located in the north of Berlin, the 178-square-metre clinic occupies a former pharmacy. The architects completely cleared and reconfigured the floor plan, optimising the flow of patients through different spaces.

Textiled tiles line wet rooms and other surfaces that are likely to be touched often, while the yellow-toned floor was cast from a plant-based resin. This floor was the biggest challenge of the project.
“A surface like this needs a perfect substrate, because every irregularity underneath would become visible,” said Batek.
“Preparing the subfloor required great precision, but it was essential for the continuous yellow to work as one uninterrupted surface.”
The architects completed the design by picking out a few elements in red, matching the sign on the wall of the reception area.
These include room numbers, chairs and signs indicating toothbrushing areas.
Cabinets are integrated into the walls, allowing tools and equipment to be hidden away.
“The space is reduced but never cold,” added Batek. “Above all, it reflects the personality of the client and her way of working with young patients.”
The studio has previously also revamped the T7.2 dental clinic in Berlin and renovated a historic cinema in the same city.
